extracted.intended_audience: U.S. Patent Office personnel / patent examiners
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for evaluating and articulating obviousness rejections under 35 U.S.C. 103, including how to analyze combinations of prior art, substitutions, analogous art, teach-away, predictability, and secondary considerations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Predictability of results from combining prior art elements
rubrics_metrics.description: A proper rejection based on combining known prior art elements includes a finding that results flowing from the combination would have been predictable to a person of ordinary skill in the art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: As explained (Crocs, Sundance, DePuy): merely pointing to presence of all claim elements in the prior art is not a complete obviousness rejection — Office personnel must find that the combination would have produced predictable results. If results would not have been predictable, do not use the combination rationale and withdraw such a rejection if entered.

rubrics_metrics.name: Elements must be expected to maintain respective properties/functions after combination
rubrics_metrics.description: One of ordinary skill would reasonably have expected the elements to maintain their respective properties or functions after they have been combined.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sundance example: hallmark of a proper combination-based rejection is that a person of ordinary skill would expect the constituent elements to perform in the same way after combination as before and to maintain their advantageous properties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Predictability includes working for intended purpose
rubrics_metrics.description: Predictable result covers not only physical combinability but also the expectation that the combination would have worked for its intended purpose.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: DePuy/other cases: the 'predictable result' refers to the expectation the combination would achieve the claimed function; if the prior art teaches away from achieving that purpose, predictability may be lacking.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clear articulation of reason(s) to combine (no conclusory statements)
rubrics_metrics.description: Rejections on obviousness cannot be sustained by mere conclusory statements; there must be some articulated reasoning with a rational underpinning to support the legal conclusion of obviousness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cite KSR and In re Kahn: Office personnel should provide a reasoned explanation for every obviousness rejection, explicitly stating the rationale for why the claimed invention would have been obvious.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of common sense and logic in motivation to combine
rubrics_metrics.description: KSR permits recourse to logic, judgment, and common sense in assessing whether there was a motivation to combine references; factfinders may resolve the issue without expert testimony where appropriate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Wyers/MPEP: the ultimate inference as to motivation to combine may boil down to 'common sense' in appropriate cases, but Office personnel must still explain why common sense supports the conclusion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Apparent reason to combine plus technical ability to optimize
rubrics_metrics.description: An 'apparent reason to combine' together with the person of ordinary skill's capability to optimize parameters can support a finding of obviousness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ecolab: where a second reference taught a parameter (e.g., pressure) that would improve effectiveness and an ordinarily skilled artisan would know how to adjust parameters, combining the teachings may be obvious. Consider whether optimization was within ordinary skill and whether there was a reasonable expectation of success.

rubrics_metrics.name: Teaching away by the prior art
rubrics_metrics.description: If the prior art discourages or counsels against the proposed combination or modification, it may 'teach away' and weigh against a finding of obviousness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Crocs and DePuy examples: where prior art explicitly describes a material or feature as unsuitable or warns of failure/inoperability, a person of ordinary skill would be deterred from making the proposed modification; teaching away supports nonobviousness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Analogous art: pertinence of references from other fields
rubrics_metrics.description: References from a different field may be considered analogous art if they are reasonably pertinent to the problem addressed by the inventor's device or method.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: ICON, Wyers: when determining analogous art, consider the problem to be solved. KSR directs a broad construction of analogous art. A reference may be reasonably pertinent even if outside the inventor's field of endeavor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not ignore modifications one skilled in the art would make
rubrics_metrics.description: An assessment must consider the modifications that an ordinarily skilled artisan would make when adapting prior art elements to a particular application; absence of such consideration may misstate teach-away or inoperability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: ICON: if a reference does not teach that a combination is undesirable, it cannot be said to teach away; also, alleged inoperability should account for routine sizing or other modifications an artisan would perform.

rubrics_metrics.name: Simple substitution of one known element for another (requirements)
rubrics_metrics.description: To reject based on simple substitution, Office personnel must resolve the Graham factual inquiries and make specific findings about the substitution and predictability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Required findings (verbatim structure provided): (1) a finding that the prior art contained a device (method, product, etc.) which differed from the claimed device by the substitution of some components (step, element, etc.) with other components; (2) a finding that the substituted components and their functions were known in the art; (3) a finding that one of ordinary skill in the art could have substituted one known element for another, and the results of the substitution would have been predictable; and (4) whatever additional findings based on the Graham factual inquiries may be necessary, in view of the facts of the case under consideration, to explain a conclusion of obviousness. If any of these findings cannot be made, the substitution rationale cannot be used.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reasonable expectation of success vs 'obvious to try'
rubrics_metrics.description: An obviousness conclusion should not rest on a bare 'obvious to try' rationale absent a reasonable expectation of success; obviousness does not require absolute predictability, but reasonable expectation is needed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In re O'Farrell and other cases: 'Obvious to try' without more is insufficient; courts look for a reasonable expectation that the attempted substitution or modification would succeed given the level of skill and the teachings of the prior art.

rubrics_metrics.name: Capabilities of a person of ordinary skill (optimization and predictability)
rubrics_metrics.description: When evaluating obviousness consider what a person of ordinary skill would have known and could have done (e.g., adjusting parameters, optimizing conditions), because such capabilities affect predictability and obviousness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ecolab and related discussions: admissions or evidence that skilled artisans would know how to optimize parameters can support an obviousness finding; conversely, if optimization was beyond ordinary skill, the outcome may differ.

rubrics_metrics.name: Secondary considerations must have a nexus to the claimed invention
rubrics_metrics.description: Objective indicia of nonobviousness (e.g., skepticism by experts, copying, praise, commercial success) require a nexus to the claimed invention and to the claim scope to be given substantial weight.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Muniauction/Leapfrog examples: where the proffered evidence is not coextensive with the claims or lacks a nexus to the claimed features, it is entitled to less weight in overcoming an obviousness case.

rubrics_metrics.name: Chemical arts / lead compound analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: In chemical cases, structural similarity and identification of a lead compound can provide a reason to modify prior art, but the examiner must identify motivation to select and modify the lead compound and whether there was an expectation of similar properties.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aventis, Eisai: motivation need not be explicit in the art and can come from many sources, but there must be some reason that would have led one of ordinary skill to select and modify a known compound. The requisite motivation can be implicit in a 'sufficiently close relationship' creating an expectation of similar properties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unknown problems disclosed by patentee can alter obviousness analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: If the patentee discovered a previously unknown problem that the prior art did not address or mention, there may have been no reason for a person of ordinary skill to make the claimed modification, supporting nonobviousness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Omeprazole example: where prior art failed to mention a stability problem (even if a theoretical reason existed), discovery of that problem by the patentee can explain why a routine modification (e.g., adding a subcoating) would not have been made by those of ordinary skill.
